lesson.title: A Charter Turned Into a Self-Governing Commonwealth
lesson.summary: Massachusetts Bay began as an ordinary trading company charter but became something unprecedented when its Puritan leaders carried the charter itself to New England, building a colony governed largely on its own terms and organized around church membership.
lesson.body:
Massachusetts Bay started, on paper, like many other English colonial ventures: a joint stock company chartered by King Charles I in 1629 to conduct trade and settlement in New England. What made this charter unusual, whether by legal oversight or deliberate design, was that it did not require the company to keep its governing body and records in England. Puritan leaders recognized the opportunity this created and arranged to bring the charter itself across the Atlantic, meaning the colony's government could operate in Massachusetts largely free of direct oversight from officials in London, an arrangement that gave the colony an unusual degree of self-rule for an English possession.

John Winthrop, who had led the 1630 fleet that carried the Great Migration's largest single wave of Puritan settlers, served as governor for much of the colony's first two decades, and his vision of the colony as a city upon a hill, a model Christian community whose success or failure the world would watch, shaped how its leaders approached governance. The colony's General Court functioned as its legislature, but political participation was tied directly to religious status: only male church members in good standing, called freemen, could vote or hold office, making Massachusetts Bay something close to a theocracy in which civic and religious authority were deliberately intertwined rather than separated.

That tight fusion of church and government produced conflict almost immediately, and some of the colony's most consequential early history involves the people it expelled. Roger Williams, a minister who argued for separating church and civil government and for fairer treatment and purchase, rather than simple seizure, of Native American land, was banished in 1635 and went on to found Providence in 1636, the settlement that became Rhode Island, on principles of religious liberty that Massachusetts explicitly rejected. Anne Hutchinson, who held religious meetings in her home and challenged ministerial authority during the Antinomian Controversy, was banished in 1637 and 1638 and helped establish another Rhode Island settlement, at Portsmouth. Both banishments reveal how narrowly Massachusetts Bay defined acceptable dissent even within a colony founded by people who had themselves fled religious persecution.

Economically, Massachusetts Bay grew well beyond its religious origins. Fishing, shipbuilding, and Atlantic trade, including trade connected to the broader colonial economy that involved sugar, rum, and enslaved labor in the Caribbean, made Boston and other Massachusetts ports increasingly prosperous and commercially sophisticated over the seventeenth century, even as the colony's formal governance remained rooted in its Puritan founding.

The colony's unusual self governing arrangement did not last indefinitely. Conflicts with the English crown over trade regulation and colonial autonomy led to the revocation of the original 1629 charter in 1684. A new royal charter issued in 1691 replaced it, merging Massachusetts Bay with Plymouth Colony into a single royal province and, significantly, replacing church membership with property ownership as the basis for voting rights, formally ending the religious test that had defined the colony's first six decades. Even so, the Puritan institutions, values, and town based governance that Massachusetts Bay had established during those decades left a lasting imprint on New England society long after the theocratic charter itself was gone.
